title: Senior's toolkit: chains of trust
summary: See the chain a server really sends, verify it against a root, and find out what a client trusts.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: chains of trust
steps.body: Most "certificate not trusted" tickets are a missing intermediate or a missing root. These commands show which one, in a minute.

toolkit.what: Connects like a client and prints every certificate the server sends, plus the verify result.
flags: send SNI; without it many servers return a default certificate
print the whole chain, not just the leaf
close the connection right after the handshake
toolkit.when: any TLS error from a client

toolkit.what: Checks a chain offline, exactly as a client would, and says which link breaks.
flags: intermediates to build the path with (not trusted by themselves)

toolkit.what: Walk a chain by hand: each certificate's issuer must be the next one's subject, ending at a self-signed root.
flags: the name of the CA above it
toolkit.example: for f in leaf.pem intermediate.pem root.pem; do openssl x509 -in $f -noout -subject -issuer; done

toolkit.what: Lists every certificate inside a bundle file. `x509` alone only reads the first one.
flags: subject and issuer of each certificate

toolkit.what: Shows the CA Issuers URL: where to download the intermediate that signed this certificate.
toolkit.when: the server forgot to send the intermediate

toolkit.what: Tests a chain against one specific root instead of the system store. Proves a private CA works before you install it everywhere.
flags: show the TLS handshake and the verify result
skip verification: for a quick look only, never in scripts

toolkit.what: Where the system trust store lives. Most Linux tools, and .NET on Linux, read this bundle.

steps.prompt: Match each option to its job.
pairs: sends SNI so the server picks the right certificate
prints every certificate the server sent
intermediates used to build the path
makes curl trust only this CA

steps.prompt: Browsers open `https://shop.example.com` fine, but your .NET service on Linux fails with `UntrustedRoot`/`PartialChain`, and so does `curl`. `s_client -showcerts` prints only one certificate. What is wrong?
options: The server sends only the leaf; configure it to send the intermediate too (serve `fullchain.pem`)
The root CA is missing from every browser
The certificate has the wrong name
steps.explain: Browsers often fill the gap from a cache or by fetching the AIA URL; most other clients do not. A server must send leaf plus intermediates. Never the root: clients already have it.

steps.prompt: Verify `api.pem` against your company root, with the intermediate in a separate file.
steps.explain: `-CAfile` holds what you trust; `-untrusted` holds the intermediates that only help build the path. Swap them and you would trust the intermediate as an anchor.

steps.prompt: A client reports "certificate not trusted". Put the triage in order.
lines: count the certificates sent and read each subject and issuer
if the intermediate is missing, fetch it from the leaf's AIA URL and fix the server's chain file

steps.prompt: Which certificates should a server send in its handshake?
items: the intermediate that signed the leaf
a certificate for a different host

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: When anything says "not trusted", run `s_client -showcerts` before you touch config, and count the certificates. Before deploying a new `fullchain.pem`, list it with `pkcs7 -print_certs` and run `openssl verify` on it.
